claims.text: The starting material is nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a single-phase, solutionized solid-solution state.
The solutionized CoCrFeNiTi has a random elemental distribution with minimal short-range order.
The starting CoCrFeNiTi state has high plasticity and favorable machinability but relatively low hardness and yield strength.
The low hardness and strength of near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi are governed by a lack of significant short-range chemical ordering.
A random elemental distribution facilitates wide dissociation of dislocations.
The random elemental distribution enables easy dislocation cross-slip.
Easy dislocation motion limits the formation of effective dislocation obstacles during deformation and therefore produces low strength.
A mild aging treatment can produce measurable short-range order in CoCrFeNiTi.
The proposed aging treatment can generate short-range order without forming secondary phases.
Short-range ordered clusters locally distort the lattice.
Short-range order raises barriers to dislocation glide.
Aging-induced short-range order impedes cross-slip and promotes dislocation interactions in CoCrFeNiTi.
The short-range-order-enhanced alloy will have greater hardness than the solutionized alloy.
The short-range-order-enhanced alloy will have greater yield strength than the solutionized alloy.
Increasing short-range order will slightly reduce ductility.
The strength increase may be modest when the induced short-range order is slight.
The proposed mechanism applies to near-equimolar, single-solid-solution CoCrFeNiTi under room-temperature or moderate deformation conditions and before second-phase precipitation.
Residual lattice distortion may also contribute to the mechanical response.
A controlled comparison of solutionized and aged samples can test the hypothesis using hardness, yield strength, short-range order, and dislocation-behavior measurements.

Failure of confirmed SRO induction to produce a statistically significant hardness or yield-strength increase together with any detectable change in dislocation behavior would falsify the proposed mechanism.
